questions.question: Explain the difference between a bar graph and a histogram, using the transport survey (240 learners) and the data-spend survey (80 learners) as your examples. State one reading you can take from each.
questions.expected_answer: A bar graph displays categorical data — labels such as walk, taxi, bus and car — so the bars are drawn with gaps between them and their order may be rearranged without changing the meaning. In the transport survey the bars stand at 96, 84, 36 and 24, totalling 240 learners; the tallest bar names the modal category, walking, and 96 out of 240 is 40 percent of the learners. A histogram displays continuous numerical data grouped into class intervals, so the bars touch and the order is fixed, because the horizontal axis is a number line. In the data-spend survey the frequencies are 12, 18, 26, 16 and 8, totalling 80 learners; the tallest bar identifies the modal class, R100 up to R150 — a class, not a single value, because the individual amounts are lost once the data are grouped. The quickest test is the horizontal axis: labels mean gaps, numbers in order mean the bars touch.

questions.question: A household's monthly income of R15 000 is shown on a pie chart. Transport occupies a sector of 54 degrees. Calculate the rand amount spent on transport, show how the angle for food at 30 percent is obtained, and state two limitations of pie charts.
questions.expected_answer: Transport: the sector is 54 out of 360 degrees, and 54 ÷ 360 = 0,15, so transport takes 15 percent of the income. Fifteen percent of R15 000 = 0,15 × R15 000 = R2 250. Food: a full revolution is 360 degrees and the whole is 100 percent, so every 1 percent is 3,6 degrees; 30 × 3,6 = 108 degrees. The angles of all sectors must total exactly 360 degrees and the percentages must total 100 — both are compulsory checks. First limitation: a pie chart shows proportions only, so unless the R15 000 total is printed somewhere on the display, no sector can be converted into rands. Second limitation: two pie charts cannot be compared slice for slice unless their totals are equal — a 30 percent food slice of R15 000 is R4 500 while a 30 percent food slice of R7 500 is only R2 250, yet the two slices look identical.

questions.question: A newspaper redraws the May and June electricity figures (410 and 450 units) on a vertical axis starting at 390, under the headline "Winter electricity use triples". Explain what is wrong, calculate the honest figure, and describe how a full answer to a "criticise this graph" question should be structured.
questions.expected_answer: The vertical axis has been truncated — it begins at 390 instead of 0 — so only the part of each bar above 390 is visible. June shows 60 units above the axis against May's 20, making June's bar look three times as tall when the quantities differ far less. The honest figure: the increase is 450 − 410 = 40 units, and 40 ÷ 410 ≈ 0,098, which is about a 9,8 percent increase, not a tripling. A full answer follows three moves: identify the feature (the truncated vertical axis), explain the distortion it creates for the reader (it exaggerates the difference between the bars), and supply the correct number (an increase of about 9,8 percent). The same three moves apply to the other tricks — unevenly spaced axes, tilted three-dimensional pie charts, pictograms scaled in both height and width, a conveniently trimmed time window, or percentages quoted without the total.
